Thus every off-diagonal coefficient of $Te_s$ vanishes, so completeness of the specified orthonormal basis implies $Te_s=c_s e_s$ for some scalar $c_s$. The representation and completion are under the exact Countable Choice hypothesis A1.

derivations.claim: The finite Hermitian spectral calculus [F11] diagonalizes $h$ with real eigenvalues; exponentiating them gives $Z>0$ and a positive trace-one matrix $r$. For nested finite regions $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$, the product-basis trace factorization and $\operatorname{Tr}r=1$ give $\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}(r^{\otimes\Lambda'})=r^{\otimes\Lambda}$. Thus the family is consistent, and [F5] defines a unique state $\omega_r$ with the displayed local restrictions.

Let $\Lambda_n=[-n,n]^d\cap\Gamma$. In a finite-volume product eigenbasis, $H_{\Lambda_n}=\sum_{x\in\Lambda_n}h_x$ has eigenvalues equal to sums of the corresponding one-site eigenvalues by [F11]. Therefore $e^{-\beta H_{\Lambda_n}}=(e^{-\beta h})^{\otimes\Lambda_n}$ and its partition function is $Z^{|\Lambda_n|}$, so its normalized Gibbs density is $r^{\otimes\Lambda_n}$. For every finite $X\subseteq\Gamma$, define $$\rho_X^{(n)}:=\operatorname{Tr}_{(X\cup\Lambda_n)\setminus X}\!\left(r^{\otimes\Lambda_n}\otimes(q^{-1}I)^{\otimes(X\setminus\Lambda_n)}\right),$$ placing the tensor factors on $\Lambda_n$ and $X\setminus\Lambda_n$ respectively. These densities are consistent: removing a site outside $\Lambda_n$ traces a factor $q^{-1}I$ to $1$, while tracing sites in $\Lambda_n$ commutes with the displayed partial trace because both are finite tensor-basis sums. Therefore [F5] gives an algebraic state $\omega_n$ on $\mathcal A$. If $A$ is local in $\mathcal A_X$, then for all sufficiently large $n$, $X\subseteq\Lambda_n$ and $\omega_n(A)=\omega_r(A)$. For arbitrary $A\in\mathcal A$, choose local $C$ with $\|A-C\|<\varepsilon/4$ using [F2]; since both states have norm one, $|\omega_n(A)-\omega_r(A)|\le2\|A-C\|+|\omega_n(C)-\omega_r(C)|<\varepsilon$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Hence $\omega_n\to\omega_r$ pointwise on $\mathcal A$.

Applying the local-pair conclusion of [F7] to this particular pointwise-convergent finite Gibbs sequence gives, for every local $C,D$, a bounded continuous strip function $F_{C,D}$, holomorphic inside, with lower and upper edges $\omega_r(C\alpha_t(D))$ and $\omega_r(\alpha_t(D)C)$. This is precisely the local conclusion of [F7]; no whole-algebra KMS conclusion is attributed to that supplier.

Let $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and choose local sequences $A_n\to A$, $B_n\to B$. On either boundary, the correlation difference for local pairs is bounded by $$\|A_n-A_m\|\,\|B_n\|+\|A_m\|\,\|B_n-B_m\|,$$ because $\omega_r$ has norm one and $\alpha_t$ is isometric by [F4]. Decomposing the difference into the two local-pair differences $(A_n-A_m,B_n)$ and $(A_m,B_n-B_m)$, [F8] gives the same bound throughout the strip; its zero-edge uniqueness makes this decomposition equal to $F_{A_n,B_n}-F_{A_m,B_m}$. The right side tends to zero, since the convergent sequences have bounded norms. Thus $F_{A_n,B_n}$ is uniformly Cauchy on the closed strip. Its limit $F_{A,B}$ is bounded and continuous there and is holomorphic inside by [F10]. Norm continuity of $\omega_r$, $\alpha_t$, and multiplication gives the required lower and upper boundary values. Therefore $\omega_r$ is KMS for all $A,B\in\mathcal A$.

derivations.claim: For $s\in S_{\mathrm{fin}}$ and finite $F\subseteq\Gamma$, let $P_F^s\in\mathcal A_F$ be the projection onto the one-dimensional local basis vector with configuration $s|_F$. If $t\in S_{\mathrm{fin}}$, then $\pi(P_F^s)e_t=e_t$ exactly when $t|_F=s|_F$, and otherwise it is zero. Thus, as $F$ increases over finite subsets ordered by inclusion, $\pi(P_F^s)$ decreases strongly to the rank-one projection $E_s:=|e_s\rangle\langle e_s|$: each basis vector $e_t$ with $t\ne s$ eventually fails at a site where it differs from $s$, and $e_s$ remains fixed. Since all these projections have norm at most one and the finite span of the basis is dense, convergence on basis vectors extends to strong convergence on every vector.

Let $k_s:=|\{x:s_x\ne0\}|$. Once $F$ contains this finite support, the product-state expectation is
$$\omega_r(P_F^s)=\prod_{x\in F}\langle s_x,r s_x\rangle=\left(\prod_{x:s_x\ne0}\langle s_x,r s_x\rangle\right)p_0^{\,|F|-k_s}.$$
Because $0<p_0<1$ and $\Gamma$ is infinite, this tends to zero along the directed set of finite regions: for every $N$ all sufficiently large $F$ have $|F|-k_s\ge N$.

Suppose a normal state $\widetilde\omega$ on $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_{\mathrm{vac}})$ extended $\omega_r$. The complements $Q_F:=I-\pi(P_F^s)$ are increasing projections. The projection onto the closure of the union of their increasing ranges is their least upper bound: it dominates each $Q_F$, and any upper bound dominates that closed span. Strong convergence in step 1.1 identifies this supremum as $I-E_s$. Normality and step 1.2 give
$$\widetilde\omega(I-E_s)=\sup_F\widetilde\omega(I-\pi(P_F^s))=\sup_F\bigl(1-\omega_r(P_F^s)\bigr)=1,$$
so $\widetilde\omega(E_s)=0$ for every $s\in S_{\mathrm{fin}}$. For finite $J\subseteq S_{\mathrm{fin}}$, the projections $R_J:=\sum_{s\in J}E_s$ increase to $I$ as $J$ ranges over finite subsets, because $(e_s)$ is a complete orthonormal basis. Applying normality again gives
$$1=\widetilde\omega(I)=\sup_J\widetilde\omega(R_J)=0,$$
a contradiction. Therefore no normal extension exists.

Suppose instead a positive trace-class density $\rho$ represented an extension. By [F4], for each $s$ and finite $F$,
$$\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\pi(P_F^s))=\sum_j\lambda_j\langle\pi(P_F^s)u_j,u_j\rangle.$$
For every fixed $N$, strong convergence in step 1.1 makes the first $N$ terms converge to $\sum_{j\le N}\lambda_j\langle E_su_j,u_j\rangle$. The tails of both the $\pi(P_F^s)$ sum and its proposed $E_s$ limit are bounded by $\sum_{j>N}\lambda_j$, because each operator is a projection. Hence their tail difference is at most $2\sum_{j>N}\lambda_j$, which tends to zero; therefore $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\pi(P_F^s))\to\operatorname{Tr}(\rho E_s)$. Step 1.2 then gives $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho E_s)=0$ for each $s$. The same finite-tail argument applied to $R_J\uparrow I$ gives $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho I)=\sup_J\operatorname{Tr}(\rho R_J)=0$, contradicting $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. Thus no such trace-class density exists.

derivations.claim: The finite linear span of $(e_s)$ is contained in $D(H_{\mathrm{vac}})$ and is dense, so $H_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is densely defined. Its diagonal eigenvalues $\epsilon N(s)$ are real, hence $\langle H_{\mathrm{vac}}\psi,\varphi\rangle=\langle\psi,H_{\mathrm{vac}}\varphi\rangle$ for $\psi,\varphi\in D(H_{\mathrm{vac}})$ by Cauchy–Schwarz. Thus it is symmetric.

Define $U_t e_s=e^{it\epsilon N(s)/\hbar}e_s$; this is unitary because every diagonal coefficient has modulus one. A local matrix coefficient between $e_s$ and $e_t$ can be nonzero only if $s$ and $t$ agree outside its finite support $\Lambda$. In that case $N(t)-N(s)=\sum_{x\in\Lambda}(\mathbf 1_{\{t_x=1\}}-\mathbf 1_{\{s_x=1\}})$, so conjugation by $U_t$ multiplies the coefficient by the same phase as conjugation by the finite onsite Hamiltonian $H_\Lambda=\epsilon\sum_{x\in\Lambda}|1\rangle\langle1|_x$. Thus $U_t\pi(A)U_t^*=\pi(\alpha_t(A))$ for every local $A$; this operator identity extends to $\mathcal A$ by norm continuity.

For each $x\in\mathbb Z$, the one-excitation configuration $s^{(x)}$ with $s_x^{(x)}=1$ and all other labels $0$ contributes $e^{-\beta\epsilon}$ to $Z_{\mathrm{vac}}(\beta)$. These configurations are distinct, so for any $m$ distinct sites the finite subsum is $m e^{-\beta\epsilon}$. Since $\epsilon,\beta>0$, this grows without bound as $m\to\infty$, and $Z_{\mathrm{vac}}(\beta)=+\infty$.

If $\varphi\in D(H_{\mathrm{vac}}^*)$, then by [F2] there is $\eta\in\ell^2(S_{\mathrm{fin}})$ such that $\langle H_{\mathrm{vac}}\psi,\varphi\rangle=\langle\psi,\eta\rangle$ for every $\psi\in D(H_{\mathrm{vac}})$. Taking $\psi=e_s$ gives $\eta_s=\epsilon N(s)\varphi_s$ for every $s$, so $(\epsilon N(s)\varphi_s)_s\in\ell^2(S_{\mathrm{fin}})$ and $\varphi\in D(H_{\mathrm{vac}})$. Conversely, if $\varphi\in D(H_{\mathrm{vac}})$, the diagonal sums satisfy $\langle H_{\mathrm{vac}}\psi,\varphi\rangle=\langle\psi,H_{\mathrm{vac}}\varphi\rangle$ for all $\psi\in D(H_{\mathrm{vac}})$, hence $H_{\mathrm{vac}}^*\varphi=H_{\mathrm{vac}}\varphi$. Therefore $D(H_{\mathrm{vac}}^*)=D(H_{\mathrm{vac}})$ and the two operators agree: $H_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is self-adjoint.

If $G_\beta$ were trace class, [F3] applied to the supplied basis $(e_s)$ would make the nonnegative diagonal sum defining $Z_{\mathrm{vac}}(\beta)$ finite, contrary to step 1.3. Thus no normalized trace-class Gibbs density is obtained from $G_\beta$. Yet [F4] gives a unique quasi-local KMS state, and [F5] confirms that it has no normal vacuum-representation extension.
